title: Automorphic Numbers Lift Uniquely: The Reduction Tower of Idempotents
description: The parent entries describe the four k-digit automorphic residues n²≡n (mod 10^k) — the idempotents of ZMod (10^k) — by COUNTING them (the base entry: exactly four; the first follow-up: 2^ω(n) in general) and by PAIRING them (the second follow-up: they are 0, 1 and a complementary pair a, 1-a with distinct last digits). None of them explains the TOWER: why the automorphic numbers grow one digit at a time, each k-digit automorphic number extending uniquely to a (k+1)-digit one (5→25→625→0625→…, 6→76→376→…). This entry supplies that structural layer. Write red k : ZMod (10^(k+1)) →+* ZMod (10^k) for the canonical digit-dropping reduction homomorphism. (1) Any ring homomorphism sends idempotents to idempotents, so red k maps the four (k+1)-digit automorphic residues into the k-digit ones. (2) The kernel of red k is a NIL ideal: every x with red k x = 0 is a multiple of 10^k, and since (10^k)²=10^(2k)=0 in ZMod (10^(k+1)) already x²=0. (3) Therefore red k is INJECTIVE on idempotents — two idempotents with equal reduction differ by a nilpotent, hence are equal (reusing the parent's idem_eq_of_sub_nilpotent). (4) Since both idempotent sets have exactly four elements (the base entry's count) and red k is injective on them, the image is the WHOLE lower set: red k is a bijection between the two four-element idempotent sets. (5) Main theorem: every k-digit automorphic residue has a UNIQUE (k+1)-digit automorphic residue lying above it. This is the precise sense in which 5, 25, 625, … is a single coherent sequence, and the reason the two nontrivial automorphic towers converge to the two nontrivial idempotents of the 10-adic integers ℤ₁₀ ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₅. The concrete reductions 25↦5, 76↦6, 625↦25 are verified by decide.

overview.historicalContext: Automorphic numbers — whole numbers whose square ends in the number itself, like $5^2=2\mathbf{5}$, $6^2=3\mathbf{6}$, $25^2=6\mathbf{25}$, $76^2=57\mathbf{76}$ — were a staple of recreational number theory long before their algebraic meaning was clear; they appear in W. W. Rouse Ball's *Mathematical Recreations* and were popularized as 'curious' or 'circular' numbers in the early twentieth century. The modern viewpoint identifies the $k$-digit automorphic numbers with the solutions of $n^2\equiv n\pmod{10^k}$, i.e. the idempotents of the ring $\mathbb{Z}/10^k$. Because $10^k=2^k\,5^k$, the Chinese Remainder Theorem splits $\mathbb{Z}/10^k\cong\mathbb{Z}/2^k\times\mathbb{Z}/5^k$, and each factor (being local) has exactly two idempotents $0,1$, giving $2\times2=4$ idempotents in all — the residues $0,1$ and the famous complementary pair (ending in $\dots5$ and $\dots6$). The deeper structure, that these solutions cohere into infinite digit-by-digit sequences, is the content of Kurt Hensel's idempotent-lifting principle for the $10$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_{10}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_5$: the two non-trivial $10$-adic idempotents are precisely the limits $\dots\,8212890625$ and $\dots\,1787109376$ to which the $\dots5$ and $\dots6$ towers converge.
overview.problemStatement: The counting and pairing companion entries determine the four idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}/10^k$ at each fixed level $k$, but treat the levels independently. This entry establishes the *vertical* structure: writing $\mathrm{red}_k:\mathbb{Z}/10^{k+1}\to\mathbb{Z}/10^k$ for the canonical reduction ring homomorphism, prove that $\mathrm{red}_k$ restricts to a bijection between the four idempotents of $\mathbb{Z}/10^{k+1}$ and the four of $\mathbb{Z}/10^k$. Equivalently: every $k$-digit automorphic residue $\bar e$ ($\bar e^2=\bar e$) is the reduction of a unique $(k+1)$-digit automorphic residue $e$, so $5,25,625,\dots$ and $6,76,376,\dots$ are single coherent towers.
overview.proofStrategy: The bijection is assembled from three ingredients without ever writing down an explicit lifting formula. (1) *Maps-to*: any ring homomorphism preserves the idempotent equation $e\cdot e=e$, so $\mathrm{red}_k$ sends idempotents to idempotents (`map_idem`). (2) *Injectivity*: the kernel of $\mathrm{red}_k$ is the ideal $(10^k)$, and $(10^k)^2=10^{2k}\equiv 0\pmod{10^{k+1}}$ for $k\ge1$, so every kernel element squares to zero — the kernel is a nil ideal (`ker_red_nilpotent`); idempotents whose difference is nilpotent must coincide (`idem_eq_of_sub_nilpotent`, reused from the pairing entry), giving injectivity on idempotents (`red_injOn_idem`). (3) *Surjectivity by counting*: both idempotent sets have exactly four elements (`automorphic_idempotent_count`, from the base entry), so an injective map between them is automatically onto — `Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le` promotes the inclusion image $\subseteq$ target to equality (`red_image_idem`). The main theorem `unique_digit_extension` then reads off existence-and-uniqueness of the lift directly from the bijection.
keyInsights: Idempotent lifting is governed by nilpotency, not by an explicit formula: because $(10^k)^2\equiv0\pmod{10^{k+1}}$, the reduction kernel is nil, and over a nil ideal idempotents lift uniquely. This is the finite, single-step shadow of Hensel's lemma for the $10$-adic integers.

Surjectivity is obtained for free from cardinality: an injection between two four-element sets is a bijection. The hard arithmetic (there are exactly four idempotents) is imported from the base counting entry; this layer needs only to supply injectivity.

The result exhibits $\{\mathbb{Z}/10^k\}_k$ as an inverse system whose transition maps $\mathrm{red}_k$ are bijective on idempotents, so the inverse limit $\mathbb{Z}_{10}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_5$ inherits exactly four idempotents — explaining why the automorphic towers converge to genuine $10$-adic idempotents.

The same nilpotency phenomenon recurs at every rung: in the parent last-digit theorem the nil element is $10$ (kernel of reduction mod $10$); here it is $10^k$ (kernel of reduction mod $10^k$). The tower is a self-similar stack of nil-ideal lifts.

Functoriality does the heavy lifting: nothing about base $10$ is special to the *mechanism* — the argument works verbatim for any modulus $m$, with the number of coherent towers equal to $2^{\omega(m)}$, the number of idempotents.

mainTheorems.name: unique_digit_extension
mainTheorems.statement: 0 < k → ē*ē=ē → ∃! e : ZMod (10^(k+1)), e*e=e ∧ red k e = ē
mainTheorems.description: Every k-digit automorphic residue ē (idempotent of ZMod (10^k)) is the reduction of a UNIQUE (k+1)-digit automorphic residue e (idempotent of ZMod (10^(k+1))). So the automorphic numbers form a single coherent tower 5→25→625→…, 6→76→376→…, converging to the two nontrivial idempotents of the 10-adic integers.
mainTheorems.significance: Explains the digit-by-digit growth left unexplained by the counting and pairing entries: the four-element idempotent set of each level sits coherently over the level below, realizing ZMod (10^k) as an inverse system whose limit ℤ₁₀ ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₅ has exactly four idempotents.

mainTheorems.name: red_image_idem
mainTheorems.description: The image under the reduction red k of the four (k+1)-digit automorphic residues is exactly the four k-digit ones: red k is a bijection between the two four-element idempotent sets. Injectivity (red_injOn_idem) plus equal cardinality (automorphic_idempotent_count, both 4) forces the image to fill the whole target.
mainTheorems.significance: The structural heart: reduction restricts to a bijection of idempotent sets, so the levels of the tower are in canonical one-to-one correspondence.

mainTheorems.name: red_injOn_idem
mainTheorems.statement: 0 < k → e*e=e → f*f=f → red k e = red k f → e = f
mainTheorems.description: The reduction red k is injective on idempotents: two idempotents with the same reduction have nilpotent difference (it lies in the nil kernel), hence are equal by the parent's idem_eq_of_sub_nilpotent.
mainTheorems.significance: Uniqueness of the lift — the second half of the bijection — derived purely from the kernel being nil.

mainTheorems.name: ker_red_nilpotent
mainTheorems.statement: 0 < k → red k x = 0 → IsNilpotent x
mainTheorems.description: The kernel of red k is a nil ideal: if red k x = 0 then x is a multiple of 10^k, and since (10^k)² = 10^(2k) = 0 in ZMod (10^(k+1)) for k ≥ 1, already x² = 0.
mainTheorems.significance: The arithmetic engine. The doubly-exponential vanishing (10^k)²=0 in ZMod (10^(k+1)) is exactly what makes idempotent lifting unique; it is the same nilpotency phenomenon that, one digit at a time, pins down the last digit in the parent entry.

mainTheorems.name: map_idem
mainTheorems.statement: (f : R →+* S) → e*e=e → f e * f e = f e
mainTheorems.description: Any ring homomorphism between commutative rings sends idempotents to idempotents (f e · f e = f (e·e) = f e).
mainTheorems.significance: Makes red k map automorphic residues to automorphic residues — the MapsTo half needed before injectivity and cardinality give a bijection.

sections.title: Part I: The digit-dropping reduction homomorphism
sections.summary: red k := ZMod.castHom (10^k ∣ 10^(k+1)) (ZMod (10^k)) is the canonical reduction ZMod (10^(k+1)) →+* ZMod (10^k). map_idem records that any ring homomorphism preserves idempotency, so red k maps the (k+1)-digit automorphic residues into the k-digit ones.
sections.mathContext: The rings ZMod (10^k) form an inverse system under reduction; red k is one transition map. Ring homomorphisms preserve the idempotent equation e·e=e, giving a map of idempotent sets.

sections.title: Part II: The kernel of reduction is a nil ideal
sections.summary: ker_red_nilpotent: lift x to a natural number m (ZMod.natCast_rightInverse); red k (↑m)=↑m=0 gives 10^k ∣ m (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff), so m = 10^k·t and x² = (10^k·t)² is a multiple of 10^(2k), which is 0 in ZMod (10^(k+1)) since 10^(k+1) ∣ 10^(2k) for k ≥ 1. Hence x² = 0.
sections.mathContext: The kernel of ZMod (10^(k+1)) → ZMod (10^k) is the ideal (10^k), and (10^k)² = 10^(2k) ≡ 0, so the kernel is nil — the hypothesis under which idempotents lift uniquely.

sections.title: Part III: Reduction is a bijection on idempotents
sections.summary: red_injOn_idem: idempotents with equal reduction differ by a kernel element, which is nilpotent, so they coincide (idem_eq_of_sub_nilpotent). red_image_idem: the image of the (k+1)-level idempotents is contained in the k-level idempotents (map_idem) and, being injective with both sets of card 4 (automorphic_idempotent_count), fills it — Finset.eq_of_subset_of_card_le upgrades the inclusion to equality.
sections.mathContext: Injective + equal finite cardinality = bijective: the four idempotents of each level correspond one-to-one with those of the level below.

sections.title: Part IV: Unique digit-by-digit extension
sections.summary: unique_digit_extension: membership of ē in the lower idempotent set, rewritten through red_image_idem, exhibits a lift e; uniqueness is red_injOn_idem. The concrete reductions 25↦5, 76↦6, 625↦25 (by decide) show the tower explicitly.
sections.mathContext: Each automorphic number extends uniquely by one digit, so 5,25,625,… and 6,76,376,… are coherent sequences — the two nontrivial idempotents of the inverse limit ℤ₁₀ ≅ ℤ₂ × ℤ₅.

conclusion.summary: Reduction $\mathrm{red}_k:\mathbb{Z}/10^{k+1}\to\mathbb{Z}/10^k$ restricts to a bijection between the four idempotents at each level, so every $k$-digit automorphic residue lifts to a unique $(k+1)$-digit one. This is the structural layer above the counting and pairing entries: it turns the four-element idempotent sets at each modulus into a single coherent inverse system, the levels of the towers $5\to25\to625\to\cdots$ and $6\to76\to376\to\cdots$ in canonical one-to-one correspondence.
implications: Identifies the two non-trivial automorphic towers with the two non-trivial idempotents of the $10$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_{10}\cong\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_5$, obtained as the limit of the inverse system $\{\mathbb{Z}/10^k\}$ whose transition maps are now known to be idempotent-bijective.
Gives a finite, fully constructive instance of idempotent lifting over a nil ideal — the engine behind Hensel's lemma — with no appeal to completeness or to an explicit Newton-style iteration.

Reduces the existence of digit extensions to a pure counting argument (injective between equinumerous finite sets ⇒ bijective), separating the arithmetic input (the count is $4$) from the structural conclusion (the levels match up).
openQuestions: For a general modulus $m$ the reduction $\mathbb{Z}/m^{k+1}\to\mathbb{Z}/m^k$ is bijective on idempotents only when $\mathrm{rad}(m)=\mathrm{rad}(m^2)$ holds appropriately; for which $m$ (beyond prime powers and squarefree-radical cases like $10$) do the $2^{\omega(m)}$ idempotent towers cohere into a clean inverse system, and what is the precise nilpotency condition on the kernel?

Can the unique lift be described by an explicit recursion on the new digit — e.g. the classical doubling map $a\mapsto 3a^2-2a^3 \pmod{10^{2k}}$ that converges quadratically to a $10$-adic idempotent — and does that Newton iteration agree with the cardinality-based existence proof given here?

What is the analogous tower picture for the *anti*-automorphic / trimorphic numbers ($n^3\equiv n$) and other polynomial fixed-point congruences, where the relevant fixed-point set need not be the idempotents of a ring?
